theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: Edge-Triggered and Master-Slave Timing

The maximum clock frequency comes from following one bit through a register-to-register path. At a clock edge the first flip-flop launches new data, which appears at its Q output after t_pd. The data then passes through the combinational logic (t_logic) and must reach the D input of the second flip-flop at least t_su before the next edge. The clock period therefore has to cover all three delays, using their worst-case (maximum) values, and the slowest path in the circuit, the critical path, sets the clock rate.

theoryAdd.plainText: Setup constraint: T_clk >= t_pd(max) + t_logic(max) + t_su

theoryAdd.text: The hold constraint looks at the same edge instead of the next one. The data launched at an edge must not reach the second flip-flop so quickly that it disturbs the value that flip-flop is still capturing. The fastest (minimum) delays matter here, and the clock period does not appear at all.

theoryAdd.plainText: Hold constraint: t_pd(min) + t_logic(min) >= t_h (independent of the clock period)

theoryAdd.text:
Worked example 1: setup and hold check
Given: t_pd = 10 ns (min 3 ns), t_su = 4 ns, t_h = 2 ns
       logic delay 18 ns (max), 2 ns (min)
T_min  = 10 + 18 + 4 = 32 ns
f_max  = 1 / 32 ns = 31.25 MHz
At 25 MHz: T = 40 ns, setup slack = 40 - 32 = +8 ns (met)
Hold slack = 3 + 2 - 2 = +3 ns (met)

To read a timing diagram, first mark every active edge of the device in question. An edge-triggered flip-flop takes the value of D exactly at those marks and ignores D everywhere else. A latch must be traced over each whole enable interval: it follows D while open and freezes the value present when it closes. Changes of D while the latch is closed appear only when it next opens.

Worked example 2: one D waveform, three devices (times in ns)
CLK HIGH 0-10, 20-30, 40-50, 60-70; D = 1 during 3-14 and 33-46
Positive-edge D FF, edges 0/20/40/60 : Q = 0, 0, 1, 0
Negative-edge D FF, edges 10/30/50/70: Q = 1, 0, 0, 0
D latch (open while CLK = 1):
  Q -> 1 at 3, holds 1 at 14 (closed), -> 0 at 20 (opens, D = 0)
  holds 0 at 33 (closed), -> 1 at 40 (opens, D = 1), -> 0 at 46

A master-slave D flip-flop can be built from two D latches with opposite enables. If the master is transparent while CLK = 0 and the slave while CLK = 1, the master tracks D during the LOW level and freezes it when the clock rises, at the same moment as the slave opens and copies it to Q: the result is a positive-edge flip-flop. Swapping the enables gives a negative-edge flip-flop. Because D latches have no feedback from Q to their inputs, this version does not show 1's catching.
Common mistakes in triggering and timing questions:
items: Using the typical instead of the worst-case (largest) propagation delay when computing f_max.
Forgetting t_su, or adding the hold time into the clock-period sum.
Assuming a pulse-triggered master-slave JK output changes at the leading (rising) edge of the clock pulse; it changes at the trailing (falling) edge.
Treating PRESET and CLEAR as synchronous: they act at once, not at the next edge.
Taking the fastest path as the critical path; the slowest path sets the clock, the fastest path decides hold.

theoryAdd.text: Lowering the clock frequency cures setup violations but never hold violations, because the clock period does not appear in the hold condition. A chip with a hold violation fails at any clock speed until delay is added to the short path.

questions.questionText: On a flip-flop logic symbol, a small triangle at the clock input indicates:
options: A postponed output of a master-slave device
questions.explanation: The triangle is the dynamic indicator: the device responds only to a clock transition, not to a level.

questions.questionText: A bubble in front of the triangle at the clock input of a flip-flop symbol means the flip-flop is:
questions.explanation: The bubble inverts the clock, so the device acts on the 1-to-0 (falling) transition.

questions.questionText: A positive-edge-triggered flip-flop samples its synchronous inputs:
options: At the 1-to-0 transition of the clock
At the 0-to-1 transition of the clock
questions.explanation: Positive edge means the rising transition; at all other times the inputs have no effect on the output.

questions.questionText: In a master-slave JK flip-flop, which latch is enabled during each clock level?
options: Master while CLK = 0, slave while CLK = 1
Both master and slave while CLK = 1
Master only at the rising edge, slave only at the falling edge
Master while CLK = 1, slave while CLK = 0
questions.explanation: The master receives the clock and the slave the inverted clock, so the master captures J and K during the HIGH level and the slave copies it to the output during the LOW level.

questions.questionText: The setup time of a flip-flop is the minimum time for which the data input must be stable:
questions.explanation: Setup time t_su is measured before the edge; the interval after the edge is the hold time.

questions.questionText: The hold time of a flip-flop is the minimum time for which the data input must remain stable:
options: Until the preset input is released
questions.explanation: Hold time t_h is measured from the active edge onward; the data must not change during it.

questions.questionText: The asynchronous PRESET and CLEAR inputs of a flip-flop:
options: Take effect only at the next active clock edge
Act only while the clock is HIGH
Select which clock edge triggers the flip-flop
Act immediately, independent of the clock
questions.explanation: Direct (asynchronous) inputs bypass the clocked input gates, so they force the output at once whatever the clock is doing.

questions.questionText: A D flip-flop has active-low PRE-bar and CLR-bar inputs. With PRE-bar = 0 and CLR-bar = 1, the output is:
options: Q = 0 regardless of the clock and D
Q = 1 regardless of the clock and D
Q = D at the next clock edge
Q toggles at each clock edge
questions.explanation: An active (LOW) preset forces Q = 1 immediately and holds it there while PRE-bar stays low.

questions.questionText: The propagation delay t_CLK-to-Q of a flip-flop is the time between:
options: The active clock edge and the resulting change at the output
A data change and the next clock edge
The release of CLEAR and the next clock edge
questions.explanation: t_pd (clock-to-Q) is how long the output takes to settle after the triggering edge.

questions.questionText: Because its output changes at the end of the clock pulse after the inputs were captured during the pulse, a master-slave flip-flop is described as:
questions.explanation: The master reads the inputs during the whole HIGH pulse and the slave updates the output on the trailing edge, so the device is pulse-triggered.

questions.questionText: When the setup or hold time of a flip-flop is violated, its output may hover between valid logic levels for an unpredictable time. This condition is called:
questions.explanation: A flip-flop sampling a changing input can be left balanced between its two stable states: metastability.

questions.questionText: The 7474 TTL IC contains:
options: Two negative-edge JK flip-flops without preset or clear
Two positive-edge-triggered D flip-flops with preset and clear
questions.explanation: The 7474 is a dual positive-edge D flip-flop with active-low preset and clear; the quad transparent latch is the 7475.

questions.questionText: An edge-detector circuit ANDs the clock with an inverted and slightly delayed copy of itself. Its output is:
options: A square wave at twice the clock frequency
A narrow pulse, about one delay wide, at each rising clock edge
A pulse at each falling edge lasting the whole LOW time
questions.explanation: Just after the clock rises, CLK = 1 and the delayed-inverted copy is still 1, so the AND output is 1 only for the length of the delay.

questions.questionText: In a D latch, a change on D while the enable is active:
options: Appears at the output after the propagation delay
Is ignored until the next rising edge
Is ignored until the enable goes inactive
questions.explanation: A latch is transparent while enabled, so the output follows D; only edge-triggered devices ignore D between edges.

questions.questionText: A D flip-flop has t_pd = 15 ns and t_su = 10 ns. Its Q output feeds the D input of an identical flip-flop directly, with no logic in between. The maximum clock frequency is:
questions.explanation: T_min = t_pd + t_su = 15 + 10 = 25 ns, so f_max = 1 / 25 ns = 40 MHz.

questions.questionText: In a register-to-register path, the flip-flops have t_pd = 8 ns and t_su = 5 ns and the logic between them has a delay of 22 ns. The maximum clock frequency is:
questions.explanation: T_min = 8 + 22 + 5 = 35 ns, so f_max = 1 / 35 ns = 28.6 MHz. Ignoring t_su gives 33.3 MHz; ignoring the logic gives 76.9 MHz.

questions.questionText: A synchronous circuit must run at 50 MHz using flip-flops with t_pd = 8 ns and t_su = 4 ns. The largest allowed delay of the logic between two flip-flops is:
questions.explanation: T = 1 / 50 MHz = 20 ns; t_logic(max) = T - t_pd - t_su = 20 - 8 - 4 = 8 ns.

questions.questionText: A circuit is clocked at 100 MHz. The flip-flops have t_pd = 3 ns and t_su = 2 ns, and the logic path between them takes 4 ns. The setup slack is:
questions.explanation: Slack = T - (t_pd + t_logic + t_su) = 10 - (3 + 4 + 2) = +1 ns, so the setup requirement is met with 1 ns to spare.

questions.questionText: For a level-triggered JK flip-flop with J = K = 1, which relation between the clock HIGH width t_p, the propagation delay t_pd and the clock period T avoids race-around?
questions.explanation: If the clock pulse ends before the output has had time to change (t_p < t_pd), the new output cannot be fed back through the still-enabled gates, so the flip-flop toggles only once per period.

questions.questionText: A negative-edge JK flip-flop with J = K = 1 starts with Q = 0. After 5 complete clock pulses (5 falling edges), Q and the number of output changes are:
questions.explanation: With J = K = 1 the output toggles once at every falling edge: 5 edges give 5 toggles, and an odd number of toggles from 0 leaves Q = 1.

questions.questionText: In a master-slave JK flip-flop, the output Q changes:
options: At the leading (rising) edge of the clock pulse
At the trailing (falling) edge of the clock pulse
questions.explanation: The slave, which drives Q, is enabled when the clock goes LOW, so the master's state reaches the output at the trailing edge.

questions.questionText: The clock is HIGH from 0 to 10, 20 to 30, 40 to 50 and 60 to 70 ns (rising edges at 0, 20, 40 and 60 ns). D is 0 until 5 ns, 1 from 5 to 27 ns, 0 from 27 to 52 ns and 1 from 52 ns on. For a positive-edge D flip-flop, Q just after the edges at 20, 40 and 60 ns is:
questions.explanation: Q takes the value of D at each rising edge: D(20) = 1, D(40) = 0, D(60) = 1. Changes of D between edges are ignored.

questions.questionText: Using the same clock and D waveforms (clock HIGH 0 to 10, 20 to 30, 40 to 50, 60 to 70 ns; D = 1 from 5 to 27 ns and from 52 ns on), a negative-edge D flip-flop gives which values of Q after the falling edges at 10, 30, 50 and 70 ns?
questions.explanation: Q copies D at each falling edge: D(10) = 1, D(30) = 0, D(50) = 0, D(70) = 1.

questions.questionText: A negative-edge-triggered JK flip-flop has Q = 0 and K = 0. While CLK = 1, J pulses briefly to 1 and returns to 0 before the falling edge. After the falling edge Q is:
options: 0, because J = 0 at the falling edge
1, then back to 0 after one propagation delay
questions.explanation: An edge-triggered flip-flop looks at J and K only around the active edge; at the falling edge J = K = 0, so the output holds at 0. It does not suffer from 1's catching.

questions.questionText: Why does a master-slave JK flip-flop not suffer from race-around when J = K = 1?
options: The slave is disabled while the master is enabled, so the outputs fed back to the master cannot change during the pulse
The master has a shorter propagation delay than the slave
The clock pulse is automatically made narrower than the propagation delay
J and K are internally forced to 0 while the clock is HIGH
questions.explanation: Race-around needs the output to change and feed back while the input gates are still enabled. In the master-slave circuit the outputs are frozen while the master is open, so only one toggle per pulse is possible.

questions.questionText: Which statement about a true edge-triggered flip-flop is NOT correct?
options: It samples its inputs only in a short window around the active edge
It is free from race-around when J = K = 1
Its inputs must be held stable for the whole time CLK = 1
It must satisfy both a setup time and a hold time
questions.explanation: Holding inputs stable for the whole HIGH time is the requirement of a master-slave (pulse-triggered) device because of 1's catching; an edge-triggered device needs stability only for t_su before and t_h after the edge.

questions.questionText: A flip-flop has t_PLH = 14 ns and t_PHL = 22 ns, and t_su = 6 ns. Using the worst-case delay and no logic between flip-flops, the maximum clock frequency is:
questions.explanation: The worst case uses the larger delay, 22 ns: T_min = 22 + 6 = 28 ns, so f_max = 1 / 28 ns = 35.7 MHz. Using t_PLH gives 50 MHz and the average delay gives 41.7 MHz.

questions.questionText: A master-slave JK flip-flop is clocked with a period of 100 ns at a 40% duty cycle (HIGH for 40% of the period). To avoid 1's catching, J and K must be held stable for at least:
options: Only the setup and hold window around the falling edge
40 ns, the whole clock HIGH time
questions.explanation: The master is transparent for the whole HIGH time, 0.40 x 100 = 40 ns, and any glitch on J or K during that time can be caught.

questions.questionText: In flip-flop data sheets, the recovery time refers to:
options: The time the output takes to settle after a clock edge
The time the output needs to leave a metastable state
The minimum time between releasing an asynchronous input (PRESET or CLEAR) and the next active clock edge
The minimum time the clock must stay LOW
questions.explanation: After CLEAR or PRESET is released, the flip-flop needs a short recovery time before a clock edge will be accepted reliably.

questions.questionText: A flip-flop requires a minimum clock HIGH width of 20 ns and a minimum clock LOW width of 25 ns. Considering pulse widths only, the maximum clock frequency is:
questions.explanation: T_min = t_w(H) + t_w(L) = 20 + 25 = 45 ns, so f_max = 1 / 45 ns = 22.2 MHz.

questions.questionText: Three negative-edge T flip-flops with T = 1 are cascaded, each Q output clocking the next stage. The first stage receives a 16 MHz clock. The frequency at the last Q output is:
questions.explanation: Each toggling stage divides by 2: 16 / 2 / 2 / 2 = 2 MHz. Dividing by 3 gives the wrong 5.33 MHz, dividing by 16 the wrong 1 MHz.

questions.questionText: On a 7474 D flip-flop, PRE-bar and CLR-bar are both driven LOW at the same time. The result is:
options: Q toggles at each clock edge
A non-allowed condition: Q and Q-bar are both forced HIGH
PRESET has priority, so Q = 1 and Q-bar = 0
Both inputs are ignored and Q follows D
questions.explanation: Each active direct input forces one output HIGH, so with both active Q = Q-bar = 1; the outputs are not complementary and the final state after release is unpredictable.

questions.questionText: A positive-edge D flip-flop has CLR-bar held LOW and D = 1 when a rising clock edge arrives. Q after the edge is:
options: 0, because the active clear overrides the clock
questions.explanation: While CLR-bar is active the output is held at 0 whatever the clock and D do; asynchronous inputs have priority over synchronous ones.

questions.questionText: Static timing analysis shows a hold-time violation between two flip-flops. The standard fix is to:
options: Add delay (buffers) in the data path between the flip-flops
Remove logic to shorten the data path
questions.explanation: A hold violation means new data arrives too soon after the edge. Adding delay in the short path fixes it; the clock period does not appear in the hold condition, so changing the frequency does not help.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a remedy for race-around in a JK flip-flop?
options: Making the clock HIGH time longer than the propagation delay
Making the clock HIGH time shorter than the propagation delay
questions.explanation: A HIGH time longer than t_pd is exactly the condition that causes race-around. The other three either break the feedback loop or limit the flip-flop to one change per clock.

questions.questionText: A positive-edge D flip-flop has t_su = 5 ns and t_h = 2 ns. D changes 2 ns before a rising clock edge and then stays constant. What happens at that edge?
options: No violation, because D changed before the edge
Both requirements are met because 2 ns equals t_h
The setup time is violated, so the captured value is unreliable
questions.explanation: D must be stable 5 ns before the edge, but it changed only 2 ns before, so setup is violated and the output may be wrong or metastable. Hold is met because D does not change after the edge.

questions.questionText: A positive-edge D flip-flop has its Q-bar output connected back to D and is clocked at 20 MHz. The Q output is a square wave of:
questions.explanation: With D = Q-bar the flip-flop toggles at every rising edge, so Q stays HIGH for one full clock period and LOW for the next: 20 / 2 = 10 MHz with equal HIGH and LOW times.

questions.questionText: Clock HIGH from 0 to 10, 20 to 30, 40 to 50 and 60 to 70 ns; D = 1 from 5 to 27 ns and from 52 ns on, otherwise 0; Q starts at 0. For a D latch that is transparent while CLK = 1, at which instants does Q change during 0 to 80 ns?
questions.explanation: Q follows D at 5 ns and 27 ns because the clock is HIGH then. At 52 ns the latch is closed, so the rise of D appears only when the latch opens again at 60 ns. 20, 40 and 60 ns would be the positive-edge flip-flop.

questions.questionText: A master-slave JK flip-flop has Q = 0 and K = 0. While CLK = 1, J pulses briefly to 1 and returns to 0 well before the clock falls. After the falling edge Q is:
options: 0, because J = 0 at the falling edge
1, then back to 0 after one propagation delay
1, because the master caught the glitch
questions.explanation: The master is a level-sensitive latch while CLK = 1: J = 1, K = 0 with Q = 0 sets it, and J returning to 0 (J = K = 0) only holds it. At the falling edge the slave copies the set state, so Q = 1. This is 1's catching.

questions.questionText: A level-triggered JK flip-flop with J = K = 1 starts with Q = 0. The clock is HIGH for 50 ns and t_pd = 12 ns. Assuming Q toggles at every whole multiple of t_pd while CLK = 1 and stops when CLK goes LOW, the number of toggles and the final Q are:
questions.explanation: Toggles occur at 12, 24, 36 and 48 ns (floor(50 / 12) = 4); the next would be at 60 ns, after the clock has gone LOW. Four toggles from 0 return Q to 0. This is race-around.

questions.questionText: A flip-flop has a minimum clock-to-Q delay of 1.5 ns and a hold time of 3 ns. The shortest logic path to the next flip-flop is 1.0 ns and clock skew is zero. The hold slack is:
questions.explanation: Hold slack = t_pd(min) + t_logic(min) - t_h = 1.5 + 1.0 - 3 = -0.5 ns, so new data reaches the second flip-flop 0.5 ns too early. Ignoring t_pd gives the wrong -2.0 ns.

questions.questionText: A synchronous circuit has two register-to-register paths. All flip-flops have t_pd = 5 ns and t_su = 3 ns; path A has 12 ns of logic and path B has 18 ns. The maximum clock frequency of the circuit is:
questions.explanation: Each path needs T >= t_pd + t_logic + t_su: A needs 20 ns, B needs 26 ns. The slower (critical) path sets the clock: f_max = 1 / 26 ns = 38.5 MHz.

questions.questionText: A design must run at 40 MHz. The flip-flops have t_pd = 6 ns and t_su = 4 ns, and each gate in the path between flip-flops has a 3 ns delay. The maximum number of gate levels allowed is:
questions.explanation: T = 1 / 40 MHz = 25 ns; time left for logic = 25 - 6 - 4 = 15 ns; 15 / 3 = 5 gate levels. Ignoring t_su gives 6, ignoring both flip-flop times gives 8.

questions.questionText: A positive-edge D flip-flop has D = 0 permanently and Q = 0. Rising clock edges occur at 0, 100 and 200 ns, and PRE-bar is pulsed LOW from 130 to 150 ns. Ignoring propagation delays, Q during 0 to 300 ns is:
options: 0 until 130 ns, 1 from 130 to 150 ns, 0 after 150 ns
0 until 130 ns, 1 from 130 to 200 ns, 0 after 200 ns
questions.explanation: The preset acts immediately at 130 ns and sets Q = 1. Releasing it at 150 ns does not change Q; the flip-flop keeps 1 until the next rising edge at 200 ns loads D = 0.

questions.questionText: A D flip-flop is built from two D latches in master-slave form. To make it positive-edge triggered, the latch enables must be arranged as:
options: Master transparent while CLK = 1, slave transparent while CLK = 0
Master transparent while CLK = 0, slave transparent while CLK = 1
questions.explanation: The master tracks D while CLK = 0 and closes when the clock rises, holding the value of D at the rising edge; the slave opens at the same moment and passes it to Q. The opposite arrangement gives a negative-edge flip-flop.

questions.questionText: Which statement about flip-flop timing violations is correct?
options: A hold-time violation cannot be removed by lowering the clock frequency
A setup-time violation cannot be removed by lowering the clock frequency
Hold time is what limits the maximum clock frequency
Adding logic delay between flip-flops makes hold violations more likely
questions.explanation: The hold condition t_pd(min) + t_logic(min) >= t_h contains no clock period, so frequency does not affect it; setup violations are cured by a longer period. Extra logic delay helps hold, not hurts it.
